chapter.name: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

questions.q: A drone starts at the origin O of a school-ground sketch and flies 3.5 m straight down the page along the vertical axis. Which pair gives its coordinates?
On Shalini's floor map, the pin E = (-2.9, 0) lies 2.9 units to the ___ of the origin along the x-axis.
questions.a: left

questions.q: A cinema ticket says only 'Row 12'. In the language of this chapter, why can the usher still not walk you to your seat?
questions.a: A row fixes a position along one line only; a second number is needed in a plane
o: A row fixes a position along one line only; a second number is needed in a plane
A row is a negative distance from the origin, so the seat's position is not fixed at all
The ticket names the x-axis but the y-axis cannot be named for a seat in a hall
Seats can be fixed by a single number only when all the rows are of equal length

questions.q: Ritu reads the history in the chapter and says, 'Coordinates started with Descartes in 1637, so nothing like them existed before.' Which reply is best supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Sindhu-Sarasvati cities had N-S and E-W streets about 10 m apart, a coordinate system in practice
o: Sindhu-Sarasvati cities had N-S and E-W streets about 10 m apart, a coordinate system in practice
Baudhayana alone wrote the 1637 rule for naming a point by two numbers, and Descartes copied it
Brahmagupta drew the first four-quadrant plane in 1637, before Descartes and Fermat did so
Ptolemy replaced Greek chords with sines in c. 499 CE and so invented the x-axis for maps

questions.q: Meenal draws a sketch of the school library on a scale of 1 cm : 2 feet. A pin marking a shelf corner is 6.5 cm from the wall that lies along the y-axis. How far is the shelf corner from that wall in the real library?
questions.a: 13 feet

questions.q: The two main roads of a small town cross at the clock tower. Taking the east-west road as the x-axis, the north-south road as the y-axis and the clock tower as O, Rani walks 400 m west of the tower along the east-west road. Where is she now?
questions.a: On the negative part of the x-axis
o: On the negative part of the x-axis
On the negative part of the y-axis
On the positive part of the x-axis

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the coordinate axes.
Statement 1: The x-axis is the horizontal line and the y-axis is the vertical line.
Statement 2: Changing the scale on the axes changes the coordinates of the origin.
Statement 3: Distances on the two axes are marked off in equal units from O.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): On the x-axis, distances to the right of O are positive.
Reason (R): On the x-axis, distances to the left of O are negative.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Tara starts at the origin and moves 6 units along the horizontal axis, towards the left. (a) Name the axis she moves along. (b) Write the coordinates of the point where she stops.
questions.a: (a) The x-axis. (b) She stops at (-6, 0): 6 units left of O is a negative x-value and the y-value stays 0.
s: Part (a): names the horizontal line as the x-axis
Part (b): writes (-6, 0) with a negative x and y = 0

questions.q: The Sindhu-Sarasvati cities had streets laid north-south and east-west about 10 metres apart. A merchant's warehouse is 7 streets east and 4 streets north of the city centre. (a) How many metres east and how many metres north of the centre is it? (b) If the centre is taken as the origin, which parts of the axes are the east and north directions?
questions.a: (a) 7 x 10 = 70 m east and 4 x 10 = 40 m north. (b) East is the positive direction of the x-axis and north is the positive direction of the y-axis.
s: Part (a): 70 m east and 40 m north using 10 m spacing
Part (b): east as positive x and north as positive y with the centre as origin

questions.q: Shalini draws a floor map 12 cm long and 9 cm wide on a scale of 1 cm : 1 foot. (a) What are the real length and width of the room? (b) How long and wide would the same room be if she redrew it on a scale of 1 cm : 2 feet?
s: Part (a): reads the scale as 12 ft by 9 ft
Part (b): halves the lengths to 6 cm by 4.5 cm

questions.q: True or False: Every point 5 units from the origin along the horizontal axis has the coordinates (5, 0). Give a reason.
questions.a: False. A point 5 units to the left of O on the x-axis is (-5, 0), since distances to the left of O are negative.
s: States False
Gives (-5, 0) for the point 5 units to the left, as leftward distances are negative

questions.q: Reiaan's room map shows only the floor. Why can the position of a window not be marked on it, and what extra information would be needed to describe a window's position?
questions.a: The map is flat, giving only positions along the floor in the x and y directions. A window is on a wall at some height, so its height above the floor (a third distance) would also be needed.
s: Says the floor map is flat and shows only x and y positions
Names height above the floor as the extra information needed

questions.q: Dev says: 'The origin always has to be in the middle of the map, because origin means centre.' Shalini placed it at a corner of the room. Is Dev right? Give two points to support your answer.
questions.a: Dev is wrong. The origin is simply where the two axes meet, and we choose that point. Shalini put it at a corner with the walls along the axes, so every point of the floor has positive coordinates and is easy to measure along the walls.
s: Gives the verdict that Dev is wrong
Says the origin is just the meeting point of the axes, placed where convenient
Explains that a corner with walls as axes gives all-positive distances along the walls

questions.q: Suppose a coordinate system had only positive numbers on its axes. Show that a point 3 units to the left of the vertical axis and 2 units above the horizontal axis could not be given its own name in such a system.
questions.a: With only positive numbers the only way to write distances 3 and 2 is (3, 2). But (3, 2) already names the point 3 units to the RIGHT of the vertical axis and 2 up. So the left point has no separate name, and the system cannot locate every point of the plane; negative numbers are needed.
s: Writes the only available name (3, 2) for the left-side point
Shows (3, 2) is already the point on the right side
Concludes negatives are needed to locate all points of the plane

questions.q: Describe a real situation of your own (not Reiaan's room) where you would set up x- and y-axes. Say where the origin is, which directions are positive, what scale you use, and give the position of two objects from the origin in real units.
questions.a: Any consistent situation, for example: a cricket ground map with O at the pitch centre, east and north positive, 1 cm : 5 m; a flag 30 m east and 20 m north, and a tent 15 m west and 10 m south, whose distances to the west and south are negative.
s: Names the origin and the two positive directions
States a scale
Gives two objects with correct directions and signs from O

questions.q: Shalini maps a school library 24 ft long and 15 ft wide on a scale of 1 cm : 1 foot. She puts the origin at the south-west corner, with the south wall along the x-axis and the west wall along the y-axis. (a) What size of sheet is needed for the floor? (b) Write the coordinates of the four corners. (c) In which quadrant do all the points of the floor lie? (d) If the origin were moved to the exact centre of the room, write the new coordinates of the four corners and name the quadrant of each.
questions.a: (a) 24 cm by 15 cm. (b) (0, 0), (24, 0), (24, 15), (0, 15). (c) Quadrant I, since all coordinates are positive. (d) Centre-origin corners: (12, 7.5) in Quadrant I, (-12, 7.5) in Quadrant II, (-12, -7.5) in Quadrant III, (12, -7.5) in Quadrant IV.
s: Part (a): 24 cm by 15 cm from the scale
Part (b): four corners with 0 and 24, 0 and 15
Part (c): Quadrant I because all coordinates are positive
Part (d): half the sides give 12 and 7.5 with correct signs
Part (d): matches each corner to its quadrant

questions.q: Section 1.1 gives a history of coordinates. (a) Who, in 1637, formalised that any point of a plane can be defined by two numbers, and what do the two numbers represent? (b) The chapter says the four-quadrant plane would be impossible without Brahmagupta's work. What did he formalise, and why does the plane need it? (c) The streets of a Sindhu-Sarasvati city were about 10 m apart. A merchant's shop is 6 streets east and 3 streets north of the centre. How far east and north is it, and how far would the merchant walk along streets from the centre to the shop?
questions.a: (a) Rene Descartes; the two numbers are the point's distances from two perpendicular axes. (b) Brahmagupta (c. 628 CE) formalised zero and negative numbers; the origin is zero and negative axes carry values less than zero, so the other three quadrants need them. (c) 60 m east and 30 m north; walking along streets means 60 + 30 = 90 m.
s: Part (a): Descartes, with distances from two perpendicular axes
Part (b): zero and negative numbers, needed for the origin and negative axes
Part (c): 60 m east and 30 m north
Part (c): total street walk of 90 m

questions.q: On Sports Day, the principal studies a map of the school ground. The school gate is the origin, the boundary wall running east is the x-axis, and the map scale is 1 cm = 5 m. The sweet stall is marked 6 cm to the east of the gate along the wall. The drinking-water point is marked 9 cm to the west of the gate on the same line. The wall runs east for 22 cm on the map. The 100 m race needs a straight clear stretch along the wall. (a) How far from the gate is the stall in real metres? (b) On which side of the y-axis is the water point and what is its real distance from the gate? (c) How long is the clear stretch of wall from the stall to the east end of the wall, and does a 100 m race fit there? (d) The principal can either run a shorter 80 m race east of the stall, or shift the stall off the wall and run the full 100 m between the water point and the east end. Which should she choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) 6 x 5 = 30 m east. (b) West of the y-axis (a negative x-value), 9 x 5 = 45 m from the gate. (c) East end is 22 x 5 = 110 m, so the stretch is 110 - 30 = 80 m, and 100 m does not fit. (d) Between the water point (-45 m) and the east end (110 m) there are 155 m of wall, so after shifting the stall a 100 m race fits with room to spare; a justified choice of the full 100 m race (the standard distance) is expected, though a reasoned choice of the 80 m race to avoid moving the stall is also acceptable.
s: Part (a): 30 m east of the gate
Part (b): west side, negative x, 45 m
Part (c): 110 - 30 = 80 m so 100 m does not fit
Part (d): decision backed by the 155 m or 80 m figures

questions.q: A model town is laid out like an ancient Sindhu-Sarasvati city: streets run north-south and east-west 10 m apart and the two main roads cross at the central square, taken as O with east and north positive. The water tank stands on the east-west road 40 m west of O. Shop S1 stands on the same road 50 m east of O. Shop S2 stands on the north-south road 30 m south of O. People may walk only along the two main roads. (a) For each of the tank, S1 and S2, say which axis it lies on and whether its distance from O is read as positive or negative. (b) How far apart are the tank and S1 along the road? (c) How far must a person walk from the tank to S2? (d) A clinic can go either 60 m east of O on the east-west road, or 25 m north of O on the north-south road. Using the total walk to the tank, S1 and S2, which site is better, and does the longest single walk change your view?
questions.a: (a) Tank: x-axis, negative (-40 m). S1: x-axis, positive (+50 m). S2: y-axis, negative (-30 m). (b) 40 + 50 = 90 m. (c) Via O: 40 + 30 = 70 m. (d) Clinic 60 m east: tank 100, S1 10, S2 90 (60 + 30), total 200, longest 100. Clinic 25 m north: tank 40 + 25 = 65, S1 50 + 25 = 75, S2 25 + 30 = 55, total 195, longest 75. The northern site has the smaller total and the smaller longest walk, so it is better.
s: Part (a): tank on negative x, S1 on positive x, S2 on negative y
Part (b): 90 m
Part (c): 70 m via the origin
Part (d): totals 200 and 195, longest 100 and 75, chooses the northern site

questions.q: In a board game, Neel's piece sits at (k, -k) on the grid, where k is a positive number. In which quadrant is the piece?
questions.a: Quadrant IV

questions.q: The point (-6, 9) is ___ units from the x-axis.
Which statement about the point (2, -7) is correct?
questions.a: It is 2 units from the y-axis and 7 units below the x-axis
o: It is 2 units from the y-axis and 7 units below the x-axis
It is 7 units from the y-axis and 2 units below the x-axis
It is 2 units to the left of the y-axis and 7 units below the x-axis
It is 2 units from the y-axis and 7 units above the x-axis

questions.q: In a treasure hunt, the clue reads: 'Stand 5 steps to the left of the wall along the y-axis, then go 3 steps above the wall along the x-axis.' Taking the crossing of the two walls as O, which pair gives the treasure's position?
Mohit is asked for the point in Quadrant III that is 3 units from the x-axis and 8 units from the y-axis. He writes (-3, -8). What is wrong with his answer, and what is the correct point?
questions.a: He swapped the two distances; the point is (-8, -3)
o: He swapped the two distances; the point is (-8, -3)
His signs are wrong; the point is (3, 8)
He chose the wrong quadrant; the point is (-3, 8)
Nothing is wrong, since both numbers are negative in Quadrant III

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: The points (-5, 3) and (3, -5) lie in the same quadrant.
Statement 2: Every point in Quadrant IV has the form (positive, negative).
Statement 3: A point whose x-coordinate is -5 may lie in Quadrant II or in Quadrant III.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The point (7, -2) lies in Quadrant IV.
Reason (R): The point (-2, 7) lies in Quadrant II.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each point in Column I with its quadrant in Column II.
Column I: 1. (4, -3)  2. (-4, 3)  3. (-4, -3)  4. (4, 3)
Column II: a. Quadrant I  b. Quadrant II  c. Quadrant III  d. Quadrant IV
(a) Name the quadrants in which A (-2, -8) and B (9, -1) lie. (b) Which of the two points is farther from the x-axis, and by how many units?
questions.a: (a) A is in Quadrant III and B is in Quadrant IV. (b) Distance from the x-axis is |y|: A is 8 units away and B is 1 unit, so A is farther by 7 units.
s: Part (a): A in Quadrant III and B in Quadrant IV
Part (b): compares |y| values 8 and 1 and gives the difference 7

questions.q: Point K has x-coordinate 6 and y-coordinate -4. (a) How far is K from the y-axis and from the x-axis? (b) A point K' is the same distance from each axis but lies in Quadrant II. Write the coordinates of K'.
questions.a: (a) 6 units from the y-axis and 4 units from the x-axis. (b) In Quadrant II x is negative and y positive, so K' = (-6, 4).
s: Part (a): 6 from the y-axis and 4 from the x-axis
Part (b): K' = (-6, 4) with signs for Quadrant II

questions.q: Point W has x-coordinate -5, and H is any other point on the line through W parallel to the y-axis. In which quadrants can H lie? Give a reason.
questions.a: Every point of that line has x = -5, which is negative. If y is positive, H is in Quadrant II; if y is negative, H is in Quadrant III. (If y = 0, H is on the x-axis and in no quadrant.)
s: Says every point on the line has the same negative x-coordinate
Names Quadrant II for positive y and Quadrant III for negative y

questions.q: True or False: The points (4, -9) and (-4, 9) lie in different quadrants. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. (4, -9) has (+, -) so it is in Quadrant IV, and (-4, 9) has (-, +) so it is in Quadrant II.
s: States True
Names Quadrant IV for (4, -9) and Quadrant II for (-4, 9) from the signs

questions.q: Three feet of a rectangular rack stand at (-3, 5), (-3, -2) and (4, -2). (a) Where is the fourth foot? (b) In which quadrant does each of the four feet lie?
questions.a: (a) The fourth foot is at (4, 5), having the x of the right pair and the y of the top pair. (b) (-3, 5) is in Quadrant II, (-3, -2) in III, (4, -2) in IV and (4, 5) in I.
s: Part (a): fourth foot (4, 5) from matching x and y values
Part (b): II, III, IV and I for the four feet

questions.q: Anand says, 'Every point with a positive y-coordinate lies in Quadrant I.' Do you agree? Give a counter-example and state what is true.
questions.a: No. (-4, 3) has a positive y-coordinate but lies in Quadrant II. A positive y-coordinate puts a point in Quadrant I if x is positive and in Quadrant II if x is negative.
s: Gives the verdict that Anand is wrong
Gives a counter-example such as (-4, 3) in Quadrant II
States the correct rule: Quadrant I or II depending on the sign of x

questions.q: Show that a point whose x- and y-coordinates have a positive product cannot lie in Quadrant II or Quadrant IV.
questions.a: In Quadrant II the coordinates are (-, +) and in Quadrant IV they are (+, -), so the product is negative in both. A positive product needs the two numbers to have the same sign, which happens only in Quadrant I (+, +) or Quadrant III (-, -).
s: States the sign pattern of Quadrants II and IV
Shows the product is negative in both
Concludes a positive product places the point in Quadrant I or III only

questions.q: Make up two points A and B so that A is in Quadrant II, 6 units from the y-axis and 2 units from the x-axis, and B is in Quadrant IV, 2 units from the y-axis and 6 units from the x-axis. Write their coordinates and explain how you chose the signs.
questions.a: A = (-6, 2) and B = (2, -6). Distance from the y-axis is the x-value in size and distance from the x-axis is the y-value in size. Quadrant II needs (-, +) and Quadrant IV needs (+, -).
s: Writes A = (-6, 2)
Writes B = (2, -6)
Explains the signs from the quadrant and the size from the distances

questions.q: The points K (6, 0), L (0, -4), M (-5, -4) and N (-5, 4) are joined in this order. (a) Say where each point lies: on an axis, or in which quadrant. (b) Find two sides that are perpendicular to each other, and name the side that is parallel to an axis. (c) Which two of the four points are mirror images of each other, and in which axis?
questions.a: (a) K is on the x-axis, L is on the y-axis, M is in Quadrant III and N is in Quadrant II. (b) LM has the same y-value -4, so it is parallel to the x-axis; MN has the same x-value -5, so it is parallel to the y-axis; LM and MN are perpendicular. (c) M (-5, -4) and N (-5, 4) have the same x and opposite y, so they are mirror images in the x-axis.
s: Part (a): K on x-axis, L on y-axis, M in III, N in II
Part (b): LM parallel to x-axis, MN parallel to y-axis, so perpendicular
Part (c): M and N mirror images in the x-axis

questions.q: A rectangular school garden has corners at (-3, -2), (5, -2), (5, 4) and (-3, 4) on a grid whose origin is the gate. (a) In which quadrant does each corner lie? (b) Show that the gate (the origin) is inside the garden. (c) Show that the garden has points in all four quadrants.
questions.a: (a) (-3, -2) is in III, (5, -2) in IV, (5, 4) in I and (-3, 4) in II. (b) The garden covers x from -3 to 5 and y from -2 to 4; since -3 < 0 < 5 and -2 < 0 < 4, (0, 0) is inside. (c) Points such as (1, 1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1) and (1, -1) are inside the garden and lie in Quadrants I, II, III and IV.
s: Part (a): quadrants III, IV, I and II for the corners
Part (b): checks 0 lies between the x-limits and between the y-limits
Part (c): gives an inside point in each quadrant

questions.q: At the school science fair, the main entrance passage runs along the y-axis of the hall plan, with the central pillar as the origin. The Robotics stall is at (-6, 4), the Chemistry stall at (-6, -3) and the Biology stall at (5, -3). The organiser wants a fourth stall, Physics, placed so that the four stalls are the corners of a rectangle. A refreshment counter is also needed. (a) In which quadrant does each existing stall lie? (b) Where should the Physics stall go, and in which quadrant will it be? (c) The counter is proposed at (0, -5). On which axis does it lie? (d) The organiser can place the counter at (0, -5) or at (3, -5). Which is better for visitors, and why?
questions.a: (a) Robotics in Quadrant II, Chemistry in Quadrant III, Biology in Quadrant IV. (b) Physics at (5, 4) in Quadrant I, the x of Biology and the y of Robotics. (c) The point (0, -5) has x = 0, so it is on the y-axis (below O). (d) (3, -5) is better: (0, -5) sits on the y-axis, the entrance passage, and would block it, while (3, -5) is in Quadrant IV, off the passage.
s: Part (a): II, III and IV for the three stalls
Part (b): (5, 4) in Quadrant I
Part (c): on the y-axis because x = 0
Part (d): chooses (3, -5) because (0, -5) blocks the passage along the y-axis

questions.q: A Pune bakery's delivery app measures every order from the shop, which is the origin. Distances are in kilometres, east and north are positive. Order A is 4 km west and 2 km north. Order B is 2 km west and 4 km north. Order C is 3 km east and 3 km south. Order D is 5 km east and 5 km north. The new clerk types each order as (north, east) instead of (east, north), so every entry has its two numbers swapped. (a) Write the correct coordinates and quadrant of Order A. (b) What does the app show for Order C because of the swap, and in which quadrant? (c) For which of the four orders does the swap not move the point? (d) The owner can ask the clerk to re-check all orders or only those that look suspicious. Using your answers, which rule should he adopt?
questions.a: (a) A = (-4, 2) in Quadrant II. (b) Order C is (3, -3) but the app shows (-3, 3), in Quadrant II instead of Quadrant IV. (c) Only Order D, (5, 5), since a point (x, y) equals (y, x) only when x = y. (d) Re-check every order whose two numbers differ, since the swap moves such a point (A, B and C all change quadrant), and skip only orders where the two numbers are equal.
s: Part (a): (-4, 2) in Quadrant II
Part (b): shows (-3, 3) in Quadrant II instead of IV
Part (c): Order D, because x = y
Part (d): rule to check all orders with unequal numbers, justified by A, B and C moving

questions.q: Four lamps stand at A (5, 0), B (0, 5), C (-5, 0) and D (0, -5). Which two lamps are on the same axis, and how far apart are they?
questions.a: A and C, on the x-axis, 10 units apart
o: A and C, on the x-axis, 10 units apart
A and B, on the x-axis, 10 units apart
A and C, on the x-axis, 5 units apart
B and D, on the x-axis, 10 units apart

questions.q: The distance between the points (-8.5, 6) and (-2, 6) is ___ units.
The point (3p - 4, 8 - p) coincides with the point (8 - p, 3p - 4) obtained by swapping its coordinates. What is p?
The point (2k - 6, k + 1) lies on the y-axis. What are its coordinates?
On a classroom plan in feet, the front wall lies along the x-axis. A door in it has one edge at (2.5, 0) and the other edge at (6, 0). How wide is the door?
questions.a: 3.5 feet

questions.q: A town numbers each crossing (a, b), where a is the N-S street and b is the E-W street meeting there. Suhana waits at the crossing (3, 6) and her friend waits at (6, 3). What is true?
questions.a: At two different crossings, since the order of the numbers matters
o: At two different crossings, since the order of the numbers matters
At the same crossing, because both pairs use the same two numbers 3 and 6
At the same crossing, because the sum 3 + 6 equals the sum 6 + 3
At different crossings only when one of the two friends is standing at the centre

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
Statement 1: A point on the x-axis has the form (x, 0).
Statement 2: The distance between (x, y1) and (x, y2) is the absolute value |y2 - y1|.
Statement 3: The points (3, 0) and (0, 3) are the same point because they use the same two numbers.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The origin lies on both the x-axis and the y-axis.
Reason (R): Every point of the x-axis has y-coordinate 0 and every point of the y-axis has x-coordinate 0.
questions.a: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Write the coordinates of the point P that is 3.6 units to the left of O on the x-axis, and of the point Q that is 5 units below O on the y-axis. (b) How far is P from the point R (2.4, 0)?
questions.a: (a) P = (-3.6, 0) and Q = (0, -5). (b) P and R are both on the x-axis, so PR = |2.4 - (-3.6)| = 6 units.

questions.q: A cupboard door in a bedroom lies along the y-axis wall from (0, 2.25) to (0, 5.75) in feet. (a) What is the width of the door? (b) A wheelchair needs a door at least 3 feet wide. Does this door meet that need?
questions.a: (a) Both ends have x = 0, so the width is |5.75 - 2.25| = 3.5 feet. (b) Yes, 3.5 ft is more than 3 ft, by 0.5 ft.
s: Part (b): compares 3.5 with 3 and says yes

questions.q: True or False: Every point on the line through (4, 0) parallel to the y-axis has x-coordinate 4, so the distance between any two such points is just the difference of their y-coordinates (taken positive). Give a reason.
questions.a: True. All such points are (4, y); the points sit on a vertical line, so the distance between (4, y1) and (4, y2) is |y2 - y1|.
s: States True
Gives the reason: equal x-coordinates, so the distance is |y2 - y1|

questions.q: In a city, the second N-S street and the 5th E-W street meet at the crossing (2, 5). There are 10 streets in each direction. (a) How many crossings can be named (4, 3)? (b) Is the crossing (3, 4) the same one? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Exactly one: the 4th N-S street meets the 3rd E-W street only once. (b) No. (3, 4) is the 3rd N-S street with the 4th E-W street, a different crossing, because (x, y) and (y, x) are different when x is not equal to y.
s: Part (a): exactly one crossing
Part (b): says different crossing, since the order matters when the numbers differ

questions.q: Find the distance between the points (-7, 4.5) and (-7, -2). State why you did not need the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem.

Part (b): 2.5 feet
Part (c): shortfall 0.5 ft and new upper edge (0, 14.5)

Part (b): 5 + 10 = 15 so collinear

(d) Route Y: shop to B = sqrt(81 + 144) = 15 km, B to A = 10 km, A to C = 6 km, total 31 km. Route X is about 1.58 km shorter. B is reached after 15 km on both routes, within 16 km, so the cake rule does not change the choice: take Route X.
s: Part (a): 5 km
Part (b): 10 km

Part (d): Route Y 31 km, picks X, notes cake reached at 15 km on both

(c) Similarly yB + yC = 2, yC + yA = 10, yA + yB = 4 give a total of 8, so yA = 6, yB = -2, yC = 4. So A (-2, 6), B (4, -2), C (8, 4).

Part (b): finds the x-coordinates -2, 4 and 8

Part (c): compares with 70 + 60 = 130 and concludes no overlap

Part (b): T outside (about 13.45) and S inside (about 11.66)

Part (d): ₹7,700 against ₹9,000 with nothing unwatered
